links.targetTitle: The Governance Point independently re-verifies the Spell aga

title: Deployment and handover each require both Spell Reviewers to approve, with test results published alongside the handover approval
content:
The Spell passes two distinct Reviewer gates. At A.1.10.2.4.10.2, Reviewers check the pre-deployment steps and "indicate their approval in a comment to the GitHub pull request, such as 'good to deploy'" — and "the Spell Crafter **may only proceed with the Spell deployment when approvals have been received from the two Spell Reviewers**." At A.1.10.2.4.10.8, after deployment and archival, they re-review the pull request, "run tests locally," and each "posts a comment approving the handover of the Spell (e.g. 'good to handover'), **including a copy of the test results**."

Staging matters because the artifact changes between the gates. The first approval covers code intended for deployment; the second covers a deployed contract at a concrete address, with archival changes applied. Re-approval means nobody's earlier signature is silently reused for a different object.

Requiring a copy of the test results is the stronger of the two demands. A verdict is unfalsifiable and cheap — "tests pass" is one line whether or not they were run. Pasted output is checkable, reproducible by anyone reading the thread, and dated, so a later investigation can see what was actually observed rather than what was concluded. It also makes running tests *locally*, as A.1.10.2.4.10.8 requires, verifiable rather than assumed — CI output alone would not show that an independent environment reproduced the result.

Two approvals rather than one means the redundancy is real at every gate: a single compromised or careless Reviewer cannot advance a Spell, which is the same two-party pattern the Atlas applies to novel designs, transfer sums and document hashes.
description: Approval is staged rather than one-shot — 'good to deploy' then 'good to handover' — and the second gate demands the evidence, not just the verdict.
